findings.passage: The difference shows in what she picks when advancement and experience pull apart, and in what she does with status once she has it.
findings.problem: The discriminator is written as observed choice, but the record holds no dated case where advancement and experience pulled apart and she gave up the advancement. In the college example she kept the lead, the producer credit and the degree, and by her own telling (S11) the price of interrupting school was a producer credit, which is an advancement term. The only offer she is recorded as ready to refuse is one without a title. Everything else under this heading is stated criteria and advice from promotional Q&As. The FAQ then states it as fact ("Type 7 leads on what she picks when career advantage and experience pull apart") and drops the body's caveats that the college reason came three years later and that college may not have been optional. Similarity lead: the diagnostic pairs this line with a bigger-route-versus-more-interesting-route sentence in another recent Seven profile (Ludwig Ahgren). I could not compare that draft, but without a Totah-specific case the frame reads as a reusable 7-versus-3 template.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the article cites one sourced, dated instance where she declined or risked a career advantage for enjoyment or experience, or the discriminator is reworded in the body and the FAQ as her stated criteria (not her picks), the text says plainly that no such test case is on record, and the FAQ carries the college caveats (reason given in 2025, may have been required, she kept the job too).

findings.passage: Totah picks jobs for "the fun," mocks her own fame, and turns bad news into a bit.
findings.problem: "The fun" is one of three criteria from a single 2024 written Q&A (S27). The draft leaves out her later and more career-minded versions of the same test: Numéro, June 2025 (S30), "where it might take me and who I might get to work with" and "work begets work," and People, 2024 (S29), "I am an actor. I want to work." The evidence record flags the 2025 line as unquoted (C18). The answer block, the type FAQ and the Why-not-3 section present the earlier, friendlier version as her standing rule, and this is one of the two legs of the discriminator.
findings.acceptance_test: The Why-not-Type-3 section quotes or accurately paraphrases the 2025 Numéro criteria, dated, beside the 2024 list and says what the addition does to the discriminator. The 60-word answer and the type FAQ no longer reduce her job test to "the fun" alone.

findings.passage: Her dream roles, listed in one breath, are "a period war drama like 1917" and "a Big Mama's House remake." A wish list built for image would point somewhere. Hers has range.
findings.problem: The source sentence continues "or a Julia Ducournau or Ruben Östlund film" (S24; C69 calls these prestige choices). Three of the four items are prestige projects, so the cut makes the list look less image-directed than it is, and the cut list is then used as evidence against Three. The section gives Three the milder half of its record in other ways. It omits "how to play the game but also how to rig it" and "I'm constantly texting and emailing people I look up to" (S24), her self-chosen "workaholic" label (S28) and "I really tried to make Tracey Wigfield, the creator, my mentor" (S30). It uses embarrassment only to rule out Eight, although the research record lists her embarrassment-and-shame vocabulary as Three material (C20, type_hypothesis.against). "Where a Three would be expected to polish it" also assumes Threes do not self-deprecate, which a comic performer of any type does as part of the job.
findings.acceptance_test: The dream-role list is quoted in full or the "Hers has range" inference is removed. At least one omitted hustle line (rigging the game or the constant cold outreach) appears with its date. The Type 3 section says once that her frequent embarrassment and shame language is itself an image-type signal. The claim that a Three would polish rather than mock their standing is removed or qualified.

findings.passage: "I was so afraid to drink because I didn't want anyone to ruin anything," she said on her podcast in April 2023, so she worked the room with props.
findings.problem: The evidence record gives the sentence as "I was so afraid to drink because I didn't want anyone to ruin anything in in my parents house" (S22 context). The draft closes the quotation before "in my parents house," which turns a teenager guarding her parents' home into a general statement of self-control. The title ("Careful Everywhere Else"), the persona title and the thesis sentence are then built on it. The same transcripts say she "always went to the bar with a fake I.D." in college (S18, noted under C24 and C56) and that she "also [doesn't] like spending money" (S22). Neither appears. Off set she also co-hosted a confessional podcast, calls herself "quite loud" (S28), and says friends greeted her gore-makeup prank calls with "This is so Josie" (S36). The record shows restraint around alcohol, possessions and exposure. It does not show someone careful everywhere else. The anecdote dates from the summer after high school, yet the fourth paragraph restates it in the present tense ("a glass she won't drink from").
findings.acceptance_test: The quotation runs through "in my parents house," or the reason is paraphrased without quotation marks and keeps the parents'-house detail. The fake-ID detail appears where her drinking restraint is discussed. The title and the thesis sentence claim no more than restraint in the specific areas the record supports. The hook is dated to her late teens and is not written as a current habit.

findings.passage: What points to Seven is the means. She took discouragement as an invitation and answered it with play.
findings.problem: Improvisation is her trade skill (stand-up at ten, hired by Wigfield for "comedy in her bones"), so a comic actor of any type would answer with it. The means does not separate Seven from Three. Her own words for the response are competitive: "a fire under my butt," "I'm going to make him love Tina," and in the same source "Honey, this is my role" and "I got it in the bag" (S38), which the draft does not quote. The outcome she reports is a larger part (he "gave me so much to play with that he didn't need to"), which is advancement. "Took discouragement as an invitation" also rests on one self-reported episode taken from a written summary of a video. The same objection applies to the Buccaneers scene: writing more material for your own character is not disinterested play.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph either supports the Seven reading with something a comic Three would not do, or says this episode does not separate the two types. It quotes at least one of the competitive lines ("this is my role" or "in the bag") or notes that the improvising enlarged her own part.

findings.passage: The same reflex shows up as a principle.
findings.problem: The type section promises that language rooted in being a closeted trans child is not counted. This sentence then counts her position on how trans and queer stories should be told as the same pain-dodging reflex as the steroid bit. That position is a representational argument, widely shared (the draft says so), and partly credited by her to others: she attributes the joy-as-protest line to a guest star (S16) and credits Katherine Jakeways with centering joy on The Buccaneers (C15). Reading a stance on trans representation as personal avoidance of pain is the causal story the draft said it would not tell. The research record leans on it heavily (C15: "the reframing move at the center of the Seven reading"), so the hedge that follows does not undo the framing.
findings.acceptance_test: "The same reflex" and any wording that treats the joy position as avoidance are removed. The position is either presented as a creative conviction that is not counted as type evidence, consistent with the limit stated in the type section, or the text explains why it counts when the box-and-freedom language does not and notes that she credits collaborators with the same framing.

findings.passage: She kept going to the bathroom at work to cry and couldn't: "I knew I needed to get out, but I could not get it out."
findings.problem: The pain-handling leg ("hard feelings get outrun instead of felt") rests on two comic set pieces from her own comedy podcast plus this story. The evidence record notes that in the same passage she says she can normally "cry at any moment" and ties the week to exhaustion and to being marginalized (C53). The draft keeps the exception and drops the rule. Across the record she reports crying, depression, anxiety and fear in public, on a show built for that, and in the finale she came back from the bathroom and said so on air. That fits someone who feels things readily and narrates them at least as well as someone outrunning them.
findings.acceptance_test: The closing section includes her statement that she can usually cry at any moment (quoted or accurately paraphrased with its source) and presents the could-not-cry week as the exception by her own account. The claim that she steps around pain is worded as a pattern in how she tells stories on a comedy show, with her repeated public disclosure of distress stated beside it as counterevidence.

findings.passage: Type 8 has the producer ultimatum and "jump on or jump off." But what she reports feeling, again and again, is fear and embarrassment, and her method with people in charge is to pitch by fib. Type 6 has the anxieties described below and a tight, loyal circle. But no single emotion makes a type, and in fourteen years of interviews there is almost no second-guessing or worst-case planning.
findings.problem: Both rebuttals assert things the draft's own evidence contradicts. "Her method with people in charge is to pitch by fib" generalizes one Buccaneers anecdote, while the One condition section shows a direct ultimatum to a showrunner at 18 ("very frank," "very upfront" in S14 and S13), and her three statements about questioning or not taking well to authority (S26, S28, S33) are left out. For Six, the hook itself is worst-case avoidance in her words ("so afraid," "ruin"). She says she recalled her mother's warning "at every instance" (S22), tried the scene on two castmates before a roundabout approach because "I was scared to do it" (S26), calls her parents her "primary sounding board" (S27), defines love as "a safety net," and says she is "tired of being scared in this world." The evidence record itself says absence of doubt in press settings is weak evidence (C73). Fear language is used to rule out Eight and is then not weighed for Six, the neighboring head type.
findings.acceptance_test: The Eight rebuttal no longer calls the fib her method and acknowledges the direct ultimatum and the authority statements. The Six paragraph lists the caution evidence (at minimum the fear around alcohol, the test-it-on-peers approach and the safety language) and either gives a discriminator between Six and Seven that is not absence of doubt in interviews or says the record does not yet separate them.

findings.passage: Josie Totah improvises on set, by her castmates' account
findings.problem: Only Alison Thornton describes improvising in scenes, in two junket interviews with Totah present (S34, S38). Boe and Dylan describe joking before takes and then locking in (S32). "Castmates" overstates the corroboration for the description's lead claim.
findings.acceptance_test: The description says "a castmate" or names Thornton, or the body adds a second named witness to in-scene improvising.

findings.passage: her read on high school in 2026, where being on television protected her: "That gave me a cachet that allowed me to survive."
findings.problem: The same Interview answer includes "People were mean to me when I was a teenager, and I was definitely mean back" (S37). It is the one unflattering thing she says about her own conduct and it bears directly on a profile pegged to her playing mean girls. The page says it found nothing from anyone with a reason to be critical while leaving out her own admission.
findings.acceptance_test: The "mean back" admission is quoted or paraphrased with its source where the cachet line or the Carrie role is discussed.

findings.passage: Neither account mentions being admired or being the best. The payoff she names is disruption and laughter.
findings.problem: The first account has her making her brother hold a flashlight pointed at her, which is wanting to be watched, and the evidence record says so (C05, C42). This is an argument from absence in two origin stories shaped for charm.
findings.acceptance_test: The "Neither account mentions" sentence is removed, or the text acknowledges the spotlight detail as attention-seeking that a Three would share.

protected_passages.passage: A person who cared a great deal would say the same thing, and it can't be checked.
protected_passages.reason: Tests her disclaimer against the obvious skeptical reading in one sentence and leaves it unresolved. This is the standard the rest of the piece should meet.

protected_passages.passage: That is praise for talent. It says nothing about motive.
protected_passages.reason: Refuses to turn an employer's compliment into type evidence.

protected_passages.passage: That reason arrived three years after graduation, and there are plainer ones.
protected_passages.reason: Dates the self-report and opens the ordinary explanations (house rules, a delayed adolescence) before the type explanation. These caveats should travel into the FAQ, not be cut.

protected_passages.passage: The read would weaken if a director or showrunner described her tracking billing, reviews or status, or if her choices after Carrie visibly favored prestige over enjoyment.
protected_passages.reason: Concrete, observable falsifiers for the leading type.

protected_passages.passage: Apart from Wigfield's one sentence, no director or showrunner describes her in their own words. This profile found nothing from her parents after 2015, and nothing from her siblings, from anyone at her high school, or from anyone with a reason to be critical.
protected_passages.reason: States the testimony gap plainly so the reader can weigh a record made of friendly sources.

assessment: The draft is more candid about its limits than most: it labels self-report, gives ordinary explanations beside type ones, handles the 2012 criticism plainly, and says who has not spoken. The weakness is that its candor is uneven. Where a limit threatens the Seven read, the adverse half of the evidence is often missing: the 2025 career-logic job criteria, the prestige half of the dream-role list, the fake ID, "in my parents house," "cry at any moment," the competitive Carrie lines and the harder hustle quotes are all in the evidence record and absent from the article. The discriminator is framed as what she picks when advancement and experience split, but no such choice is on record; it is stated criteria. The joy stance on trans stories is counted as avoidance despite the draft's own exclusion rule. Types 6 and 8 are dismissed with claims the draft's evidence contradicts. Medium confidence is defensible only if the discriminator is restated as stated criteria and the Six case gets a real hearing. Similarity: the tripped pairs are stock vocabulary (the head-triad definition, "promotional interviews," "options open"), not reused argument; the one lead worth acting on is the 7-versus-3 discriminator frame, covered in critic-01. I compared only against the diagnostic excerpts, not the other drafts. Subject is 25 with a record back to 2012, so this is correctly a standard profile, not an open case.
